claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The relatively low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi are governed by a lack of nanoscale precipitates or short-range-ordered clusters.
Nanoscale precipitates or short-range-ordered clusters obstruct dislocation motion.
Other high-entropy alloys with higher hardness and compressive strength likely obtain these properties from nanoscale features that impede dislocation glide.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution without significant nanoscale precipitates.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy lacks significant short-range order.
A controlled heat treatment can induce the nucleation and controlled growth of coherent nanoscale precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
In a uniform solid solution lacking nanoscale obstacles, dislocations move more freely.
Freer dislocation motion produces higher plasticity and machinability but lower work hardening and strength.
Heat-treatment-induced nanoscale precipitates hinder dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation motion with nanoscale precipitates increases hardness and compressive strength at the expense of ductility.
Heat-treated CoCrFeNiTi containing a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates will have significantly greater hardness than the as-cast homogeneous alloy.
Heat-treated CoCrFeNiTi containing a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates will have significantly greater compressive strength than the as-cast homogeneous alloy.
Heat-treated CoCrFeNiTi containing a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates will have lower plasticity than the as-cast homogeneous alloy.
The proposed relationship applies to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi from ambient temperature to 600 °C under typical compressive and quasi-static deformation conditions.
The proposed relationship may not apply to alloys that contain significant secondary phases initially.
Failure of the heat-treated samples to show a statistically significant increase in both hardness and compressive strength together with decreased plasticity would falsify the hypothesis.
